supplement.where: Appendices A1 to A4 at the end of this PDF (PDF pp. 27-32; printed A1-A4, then 5 and 6). The paper mentions no online supplement.
supplement.holds: Figure A1 (event-study pre-trend test), Figures A2-A3 (pre-treatment fit of Generalized SCM and Synthetic DiD), Table A1 (OpenAI-embedding similarity), Table A2 (excluding Easter weeks 14-15), Table A3 (excluding week 17), Table A4 (likes with word-count and posting-frequency covariates), Table A5 (comments). The main-text tables hold the standard errors for the four similarity measures, likes, posting frequency, and word count. Tables A1-A5 report coefficients, bootstrapped standard errors, and business-week observation counts.

paper_design_summary: The paper uses Italy's ChatGPT ban (March 31 to April 28, 2023) as a natural experiment, comparing the Instagram marketing posts of restaurants in Milan (treated) with those of restaurants in Paris, Lyon, Madrid, and Valencia (control) over weeks 8 to 17 of 2023. It estimates Generalized Synthetic Control and Synthetic Difference-in-Differences models on a business-week panel. Outcomes are each business's average text similarity to other businesses' posts in the same city and week (lexical, syntactical, semantic, language style, plus an OpenAI-embedding robustness measure), likes, comments, posting frequency, and post word count; no person is assigned to AI, and ChatGPT use is not observed.

studies.label: Italy ChatGPT ban natural experiment (restaurant Instagram posts, Milan vs. Paris, Lyon, Madrid, Valencia)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was assigned by the researchers. The Italian Data Protection Authority blocked ChatGPT for all Italian IP addresses from March 31 to April 28, 2023 (weeks 13 to 17 of 2023). The authors designate Milan as the treated city and Paris, Lyon, Madrid, and Valencia as control cities. The paper says the shock 'randomizes access to ChatGPT at the city level', but there is one treated city and no random draw.
assignment.quote: To establish a treatment and control group, we designate Milan as the treatment city and select four other European cities—Paris, Lyon, Madrid, and Valencia—as the control group.
assignment.locator: p. 6, Section 2.2 (quote and choice of cities); p. 6, Section 2.1 (ban dates); p. 12, Section 2.5.1 (treatment indicator); p. 13, Section 3 (the authors call the shock randomizing, without reporting random assignment)

arms.name: ChatGPT access
arms.description: Business-weeks in which ChatGPT was accessible (treatment indicator equal to zero): restaurants in Paris, Lyon, Madrid, and Valencia in all modeled weeks (8 to 17 of 2023) and Milan restaurants in the pre-ban weeks (8 to 12). ChatGPT use is not observed. Businesses analyzed in the 2023 descriptive sample after filtering (p. 7, Table 1, Step 3; p. 8, Table 2): Paris 429, Lyon 432, Madrid 544, Valencia 315; Milan's 486 contribute their pre-ban weeks. The estimators use these business-weeks to build Milan's counterfactual. The number of businesses entering each regression is not stated.

arms.name: ChatGPT ban (Milan, weeks 13-17)
arms.description: Milan restaurants during the ban, the paper's treated group in the treatment period: ChatGPT blocked for Italian IP addresses from March 31 to April 28, 2023 (weeks 13 to 17; week 13 commences 27 March 2023). Milan has 486 businesses analyzed in the 2023 descriptive sample after filtering (p. 7, Table 1, Step 3; p. 8, Table 2); the number entering each regression is not stated. VPN access cannot be ruled out (p. 14).

participants.exclusions: Units are restaurant businesses (Instagram accounts), not people. Collection steps (Table 1): Google Maps restaurant listings (Step 1: Milan 2695, Paris 4401, Lyon 1811, Madrid 3347, Valencia 1770), those with an Instagram link (Step 2: 752, 699, 660, 801, 468), and businesses analyzed in the 2023 descriptive sample after filtering (Step 3: 486, 429, 432, 544, 315; Table 2). Google Maps category labels were used to drop non-restaurants such as cafes and grocery stores. Kept only businesses that posted on Instagram before January 1, 2023; excluded businesses that became inactive on Instagram after April 28, 2023; removed major international food and hotel chains. The data include only posts from businesses that display like counts (footnote 5, p. 7). Language-style similarity uses only posts in each country's official language (p. 10). One negative semantic-similarity score was removed (p. 9). The main similarity analysis using Synthetic DiD uses a balanced sample of restaurants that posted every week (pp. 13, 21); this restriction should not be generalized to the posting-frequency analysis, which includes weeks with zero posts (pp. 20-22). The paper prints no total business count and no business count for any estimation sample; samples are given in business-week observations.
participants.who: Independent restaurants (small businesses) with public Instagram accounts, identified from Google Maps with Apify; their text marketing posts on Instagram
participants.country: Italy (Milan, treated); France (Paris, Lyon) and Spain (Madrid, Valencia), control
participants.quote: For each city, we report the number of businesses, along with key statistics for social media activity, including the number of posts per business, the like count, and the word count of posts.
participants.locator: p. 7, Section 2.2 (quote, inclusion criteria, and Table 1 counts); p. 8, Table 2 (businesses analyzed in the 2023 descriptive sample); p. 10, Section 2.3 (business-week observations); p. 13, Section 2.5.2 and p. 21, Section 5.1 (balanced main similarity sample); pp. 20-22, Sections 5.1-5.2 (outcome-specific observation rules)

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT (OpenAI); model version not stated; access only, use not observed
ai_tool.how_used: Not observed. ChatGPT was accessible to control-city restaurants throughout and to Milan restaurants before March 31, 2023, and blocked for Italian IP addresses during the ban (p. 6). The paper proxies reliance with cuisine origin and the drop in posting frequency: 'Since we do not observe direct usage data, we turn to two proxies' (p. 14, Section 3.1). Copilot, Gemini, and Meta AI became available in the EU only after November 2023, June 2024, and March 2025 (p. 6); VPN use cannot be ruled out (p. 14).

task.description: Real-world text of restaurants' Instagram marketing posts (captions), scraped with Apify; mean post word count 46.1 to 53.0 by city in 2023 (Table 2).
task.duration: Modeling period weeks 8 to 17 of 2023 (late February to late April); ban weeks 13 to 17 (week 13 commencing 27 March 2023; ban from March 31 to April 28, 2023).

outcomes.name: Lexical similarity across businesses (bag-of-words cosine)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Bag-of-words count vectors (stop-words and URLs removed); cosine similarity between each post and the posts of every other business in the same city and week, averaged to one score per business-week (pp. 9-10). Higher means more similar, so less diverse. Robustness variants: excluding Easter weeks 14-15, Table A2 (Generalized SCM -0.004*** (0.001), Observations 9,653; Synthetic DID -0.001* (0.000), Observations 5,136; PDF p. 30); excluding week 17, Table A3 (Generalized SCM -0.002*** (0.002), Observations 10,792; Synthetic DID -0.001*** (0.000), Observations 5,346; PDF p. 31). Subgroups: Table 5, cuisine origin (p. 16); Table 6, posting-frequency drop (p. 17).

contrasts.reported: Printed coefficients are the effect of the ban (ban minus access) on similarity. Direction is coded on diversity (sign reversed): similarity is lower under the ban, so diversity is lower with access. Generalized SCM -0.003*** (0.001), Observations 12,004; Synthetic DID -0.001*** (0.000), Observations 5,780. Text: relative decline of approximately 15% (coefficient divided by the mean of the similarity score, footnote 8). Milan lexical similarity in 2023: mean 0.020, Std 0.02 (Table 3).
contrasts.locator: p. 14, Table 4, col. (1); pp. 13-14, Section 3 text and footnote 8; p. 11, Table 3

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity of bag-of-words count vectors, averaged per business-week
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each post of a business against all posts of every other business in the same city and week; pairwise scores averaged to one score per business per week in which it posted.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Generalized SCM (business and week fixed effects plus interactive fixed effects; inference by non-parametric bootstrap, p. 12) and Synthetic DiD on a balanced business-week panel. Table notes: standard errors clustered at the city level (five cities) and bootstrapped; how the two combine is not explained.
diversity_detail.notes: Higher similarity means more homogeneous content. The estimate concerns losing ChatGPT access under a government ban; direct usage data are not observed (p. 14, Section 3.1).

outcomes.name: Semantic similarity across businesses (Sentence-BERT cosine)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Pre-trained Sentence-BERT embeddings; cosine similarity between each post and the posts of every other business in the same city and week, averaged per business-week; one negative pairwise score removed (p. 9). Robustness variants: Table A2, excluding Easter (Generalized SCM -0.007*** (0.001), Observations 9,653; Synthetic DID -0.009*** (0.001), Observations 5,136); Table A3, excluding week 17 (Generalized SCM -0.010*** (0.003), Observations 10,792; Synthetic DID -0.010*** (0.001), Observations 5,346). Subgroups, Generalized SCM: Table 5, local restaurants -0.008* (0.004), Observations 1,792, vs non-local -0.013*** (0.002), Observations 3,596 (p. 16); Table 6, high-drop -0.009*** (0.001), Observations 5,368, vs low-drop -0.006*** (0.002), Observations 6,636 (p. 17). OpenAI-embedding robustness variant (formerly S1-O5, consolidated here under form-spec Rule 7): OpenAI text-embedding-3-small embeddings and cosine similarity, aggregated using the same business-week-city strategy as the main analysis (PDF pp. 28-29, Appendix A2.1). Table A1 (PDF p. 30, printed A4) reports the ban-minus-access coefficients on similarity: Generalized SCM -0.022*** (0.001), Observations 12,004; Synthetic DID -0.011*** (0.001), Observations 5,780. Table A1 says standard errors are clustered at the city level and calculated using bootstrapping. This is an alternative semantic-relatedness measure, not a separate outcome. Table A2 is on PDF p. 30; Table A3 is on PDF p. 31.

contrasts.reported: Printed coefficients are the effect of the ban (ban minus access) on similarity; direction coded on diversity (sign reversed). Generalized SCM -0.008*** (0.002), Observations 12,004; Synthetic DID -0.009*** (0.001), Observations 5,780. Text: relative decline of approximately 2%. Milan semantic similarity in 2023: mean 0.414, Std 0.07 (Table 3).
contrasts.locator: p. 14, Table 4, col. (3); pp. 13-14, Section 3 text; p. 11, Table 3; p. 16, Table 5; p. 17, Table 6; PDF pp. 28-30, Appendix A2.1 and Table A1 (OpenAI robustness variant in measure_detail)

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity of Sentence-BERT embeddings, averaged per business-week
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Main measure: pre-trained Sentence-BERT (S-BERT), checkpoint not stated. Robustness variant: OpenAI text-embedding-3-small (PDF p. 29, Appendix A2.1).
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each post of a business against all posts of every other business in the same city and week; averaged per business-week. The OpenAI robustness variant uses every pair of posts and the same aggregation strategy as the primary analysis (PDF p. 29); exclusion of same-business pairs is not restated there.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Generalized SCM (non-parametric bootstrap) and Synthetic DiD on the business-week panel; table notes say standard errors are clustered at the city level and bootstrapped.
diversity_detail.notes: The paper's main semantic-similarity measure, the one the codebook prefers for an across_people primary record. The OpenAI robustness variant is retained in measure_detail rather than as a separate outcome; Appendix A2.1 ends mid-sentence on PDF p. 29, but Table A1 is present on PDF p. 30.

outcomes.name: Language style similarity across businesses (LIWC language style matching)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Language style matching (Ireland and Pennebaker 2010) over nine LIWC function-word categories with language-specific dictionaries (categories selected manually, footnote 7, p. 9), computed per post pair and averaged per business-week; only posts in each country's official language (p. 10). A dictionary-based function-word measure; lexical_overlap is the closest measure code. Robustness variants: Table A2, excluding Easter (Generalized SCM -0.009** (0.004), Observations 8,336; Synthetic DID -0.009 (0.006), Observations 3,936); Table A3, excluding week 17 (Generalized SCM -0.010 (0.008), Observations 9,301; Synthetic DID -0.008 (0.008), Observations 4,158), where the paper says the decline 'becomes statistically insignificant'. Subgroups: Tables 5 and 6. Appendix table locators: Table A2, PDF p. 30 (printed A4); Table A3, PDF p. 31 (printed 5).

contrasts.reported: Printed coefficients are the effect of the ban (ban minus access) on similarity; direction coded on diversity (sign reversed). Generalized SCM -0.013*** (0.004), Observations 10,354; Synthetic DID -0.009 (0.007), Observations 4,420 (not marked significant). Text: relative decline of approximately 3%. Milan language style similarity in 2023: mean 0.396, Std 0.11 (Table 3).
contrasts.locator: p. 14, Table 4, col. (4); pp. 13-14, Section 3 text; p. 11, Table 3; PDF p. 31 (printed 5), Table A3

diversity_detail.metric: Language style matching: 1 - |p_i - p_j| / (p_i + p_j + 0.0001) per function-word category, averaged over nine categories (Equations 1-2), then averaged per business-week

diversity_detail.uncertainty: Generalized SCM (non-parametric bootstrap) and Synthetic DiD on the business-week panel; table notes say standard errors are clustered at the city level and bootstrapped.

outcomes.name: Consumer engagement: average likes per post (business-week)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: log(AverageLikes + 1), where AverageLikes is the average number of likes on a business's Instagram posts in a week (pp. 17-18); like counts are a snapshot taken at the end of 2024 (footnote 9, p. 17); the data include only businesses that display like counts (footnote 5, p. 7). Variant: average like count winsorized at 5% (Table 7, col. 2). With average word count and posting frequency as covariates, Table A4 (Generalized SCM only): 1% Winsorized 4.684 (4.640), 5% Winsorized 9.393*** (3.318), Log Average Like Count 0.039*** (0.009), Observations 11,191 (PDF p. 32). Table 8 (p. 21) reports OLS correlations of log likes with each similarity measure and its square; it has no AI contrast and is not recorded here.

contrasts.reported: Printed coefficients are the effect of the ban (ban minus access): likes are higher during the ban, so lower with access. Log Average Like Count (All): Generalized SCM 0.035*** (0.009), Observations 11,191; Synthetic DiD 0.067*** (0.0198), Observations 5,070. Average Like Count (5% Winsorized): Generalized SCM 8.277*** (3.636), Observations 11,191; Synthetic DiD 8.047 (6.915), Observations 5,070. Abstract: 'an approximate 3.5% increase in average like counts'.
contrasts.locator: p. 19, Table 7; p. 18, Section 4; p. 1, abstract; PDF p. 32 (printed 6), Table A4

outcomes.name: Average word count per post (business-week)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: AverageWordCount_iw, the average word count of business i's posts in week w; no observation when a business does not post that week (p. 22). A computed count, not a creativity scoring model; no allowed measure code fits exactly, and automated_score is the closest.

contrasts.reported: Printed coefficients are the effect of the ban (ban minus access): posts are shorter during the ban, so longer with access. Generalized SCM -1.210*** (0.283), Observations 12,004; Synthetic DiD -0.637*** (0.220), Observations 5,780. Text: 'an estimated reduction of approximately one word following the ChatGPT ban'.

outcomes.name: Posting frequency (posts per business-week)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Frequency_iw, the number of posts by business i in week w; weeks with no posts recorded as 0; on average 1.34 posts per week in the modeling sample, maximum 28 (pp. 20-21). A volume measure, not a count of ideas; behavioral is the closest allowed measure code.

contrasts.reported: Printed coefficients are the effect of the ban (ban minus access): fewer posts during the ban, so more with access. Generalized SCM -0.061*** (0.024), Observations 21,530; Synthetic DiD -0.056*** (0.019), Observations 21,530.

company_involvement.description: None stated. The authors list London Business School affiliations (p. 1), and the document has no funding or acknowledgment statement. Data were scraped from public Google Maps and Instagram pages with Apify (p. 7); OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small serves only as a measurement tool (PDF p. 29).
company_involvement.locator: p. 1; p. 7, Section 2.2; PDF p. 29 (printed A3), Appendix A2.1

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is not met: Italy's ChatGPT ban is a natural experiment, and the authors designate Milan and select four control cities rather than randomly assigning people to AI (p. 6, Sections 2.1-2.2; p. 13, Section 3). The paper explicitly describes its data as observational (p. 22, Section 6). Criterion 2 is unclear: the analyzed 2023 descriptive sample contains businesses (Milan 486, Paris 429, Lyon 432, Madrid 544, Valencia 315; p. 7, Table 1, Step 3; p. 8, Table 2), and regressions count business-weeks, not distinct human producers (p. 10, Section 2.3; p. 14, Table 4). No analyzed people count is stated. Criterion 3 is met: the paper computes pairwise text similarity on Instagram posts from different businesses, then aggregates it per business-week (pp. 8-10, Section 2.3). The paper remains observational context and is not core regardless of whether the missing people count could meet the threshold.

one_line_finding: During Italy's 2023 ChatGPT ban, Milan restaurants' Instagram posts became less similar to other restaurants' posts relative to synthetic controls from Paris, Lyon, Madrid, and Valencia (Generalized SCM: lexical -0.003, syntactical -0.003, semantic -0.008, language style -0.013, all marked significant at 1 percent; relative declines of about 15, 12, 2, and 3 percent; p. 14, Table 4), while log average likes rose 0.035 (p. 19, Table 7).
open_questions: Comparison coding: this form codes the contrast as ai_vs_bau with ChatGPT access as the treatment arm and the ban as the control arm, so each printed coefficient (ban minus access) has the opposite sign to the access effect. The codebook defines comparison codes for randomized experiments; Review 1 may prefer 'other' for this natural experiment (Screener A's choice).

Question code: Milan's ban-period posts are unassisted output written after a period of possible ChatGPT access. The similarity outcomes are coded across_people (access vs. no access while writing), not after_ai, because the comparison is with posts written while ChatGPT was available. Both screeners flagged after_ai as an alternative.
Whether restaurant businesses (Instagram accounts) count toward the 50-participant rule; moot for core because criterion 1 fails.

Whether likes, comments, posting frequency, and word count belong in the creativity section at all; they are coded with_ai under the codebook rule that a non-diversity outcome produced with AI available is with_ai.
No allowed measure code fits a word count (coded automated_score) or a count of posts (coded behavioral).
Table notes say standard errors are both bootstrapped and clustered at the city level with five cities; how clustering enters the bootstrap is not explained.
notes: Two estimators per outcome, both preferred specifications (p. 11): Generalized SCM and Synthetic DiD. The text's relative percentage changes use Generalized SCM estimates (pp. 3, 14). Synthetic DiD requires a balanced panel; the paper's statement that restaurants posted every week refers to its main similarity results (p. 21), while posting frequency includes zero-post weeks (pp. 20-22). Standard DiD was set aside because event-study pre-trends fail, especially for syntactical similarity (PDF p. 27, Appendix A1.1, Figure A1). Not recorded as separate outcomes: Figure 1 (p. 12), model-free weekly similarity in Milan; Table 8 (p. 21), OLS correlations of log likes with similarity and its square; Figures A2-A3, pre-treatment fit. Subgroups (Tables 5-6) and robustness variants (Tables A1-A4) are in measure_detail. To follow form-spec Rule 7, the OpenAI semantic-relatedness variant formerly recorded as S1-O5 is now retained within S1-O3; the other outcome identifiers are unchanged. No effect size has been computed. Causal estimates are regression coefficients with bootstrapped standard errors. The Table 3 descriptives cover 2023 city samples, not human-participant arm means and standard deviations for the causal contrasts. The regression observation is one business-week, aggregating one restaurant's weekly output set; unit='set' is the closest available form code, and does not mean a person or a whole city's pool. n_units records Generalized SCM business-week observations, with the Synthetic DiD count stated separately in reported or measure_detail; the posting-frequency sets may be empty. All people counts remain null. No shared sample, preregistration, data repository, or code repository is stated. Possible document defects are retained as printed: p. 20 cites Table 2 for similarity descriptives that are in Table 3; Appendix A2.1 ends mid-sentence (PDF p. 29); Appendix A4 says the comment coefficients are positive, but Table A5 col. 2 Generalized SCM is -0.042; Table A3 col. 1 prints Generalized SCM -0.002*** with standard error (0.002). PDF pages equal printed pages for pp. 1-26; appendix pages printed A1-A4 are PDF pp. 27-30, followed by printed 5 and 6 (PDF pp. 31-32). Finalization covered the entire markdown, including references and appendices, and checked the recorded numerical values against PDF text. No c013 challenge files were present, so challenge_resolution is empty and its action counts are zero. Spec and clarity changes include grouping the embedding robustness variant, coding the business-week aggregates as sets, distinguishing analyzed business counts from people counts, and removing the unsupported intent-to-treat label. The reconciliation object is unchanged as an audit record and therefore retains the earlier separate S1-O5 and participant-unit coding. Dispositions of all original open_questions appear in final.open_items.

open_items.item: Comparison coding (open_questions[0]): retain ai_vs_bau to describe accessible ChatGPT versus the ban, with observational design recorded separately. This is a descriptive coding choice, not a randomized contrast. Printed coefficients remain ban minus access; the form's direction describes access and reverses similarity to diversity (p. 12, Section 2.5.1; p. 14, Table 4). No additional source is needed; this does not alter any eligibility criterion.

Question code (open_questions[1]): retain across_people for similarity. The analysis compares marketing output under accessible versus blocked ChatGPT across places and weeks (pp. 6, 12-14); it does not establish a period of individual AI use followed by an unassisted follow-up, and direct usage is unobserved (p. 14, Section 3.1). A carryover effect of prior AI use is not identified. No eligibility criterion depends on this descriptive question code.

People count (open_questions[2]): restaurant businesses and business-week observations cannot be substituted for people under the codebook. The number of distinct human content producers represented in the analyzed sample is not stated (pp. 7-8, Tables 1-2; p. 10, Section 2.3). Author documentation of that number would settle criterion 2; it cannot overcome the failure of criterion 1. People counts remain null.

Scope of likes, comments, posting frequency, and word count (open_questions[3]): retain these as ancillary with_ai outcomes describing engagement, volume, and elaboration (pp. 17-22, Sections 4-5; PDF pp. 31-32, Appendix A4). They are not evidence of a creativity rating. Criterion 3 is independently met by the output-based similarity measures (pp. 8-10, Section 2.3), so no further source is needed for eligibility.

Measure codes for counts (open_questions[4]): retain automated_score for computed word count and behavioral for posting frequency as the closest allowed labels, with their exact meanings stated in measure_detail (pp. 20-22, Sections 5.1-5.2). Neither label changes the output-similarity evidence or any eligibility criterion; no additional source is needed.

Bootstrap and city clustering (open_questions[5]): unresolved. Section 2.5.1 reports non-parametric bootstrapping, while table notes also report city-clustered standard errors (p. 12; p. 14, Table 4; PDF p. 30, Table A1). The PDF and included appendices do not specify how these are combined. The authors' resampling procedure or analysis code would settle the precision question; none of the three eligibility criteria depends on it.
